transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: Thu Jul 1 2026 10:00 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Julia (Redwood SE), Leo (Redwood Solutions), Mike (Nimbus Eng Lead), Priya (SRE), Daniel (ML), Alicia (PM)
Links shared: S3://redwood/poc/nimbus/kernel_sample_v3.csv, https://redwood.docs/soc2-excerpt (sent in chat), Benchmark spreadsheet (drive.link/nimbus-bench)

[00:00] Samir: hey everybody, good morning, thanks for carving out time. quick checkin, uh we're at week four of the pilot, so the focus today is convergence on TTFT and the kernel sampling approach we proposed.
[00:18] Mike: yep thanks Samir, morning. we definitely saw the smaller wins last week on average, but Priya's concerned about the 95th and 99th spikes, those microbursts, they still catch us off guard.
[00:31] Priya: yeah the alerts are coming from production-ish traffic replay we did, so not totally synthetic.
[00:40] Julia: cool, that's exactly what we expected to pop up. quick recap - we pushed kernel_sample_v2 last Thursday with lighter quantization and an early-kv-flush change, and median TTFT dropped about 18% on our harness. but the tail was stubborn.
[00:57] Daniel: can you remind me, the early-kv-flush, is that the thing that occasionally causes an extra handshake? i think i saw a note about a streaming handshake penalty at seqlen transitions.
[01:13] Julia: yes, good call. the current flush heuristics do cause a micro-handshake when the KV cache eviction hits during the streaming session. in practice it's like a 20-40ms flared latency for that particular token. for most customers that's fine, but for you where your UI cares about first-response we want to minimize those.
[01:32] Alicia: for product clarity — users consider first token as the UI spinner stop, so even small spikes look like poor performance.
[01:40] Samir: exact, UX threshold is pretty aggressive. so plan today: Julia will walk through kernel_sample_v3, which targets the microburst sources — altered kernel path selection for short seqlens and an adjusted batching guardrail. then we decide next test matrix.
[01:58] Julia: ok i'll share my screen — (screen shows slide) kernel_sample_v3 changes: 1) early-return path for seqlen <= 64 that avoids heavy attention kernels, 2) kv-cache smoothing to avoid eviction mid-stream, 3) adaptive batch cutover to prevent head-of-line blocking when there's mixed seqlen in the batch. these are heuristics layered on the runtime; not model surgery.
[02:26] [02:26] Speaker 3 (Mike): that adaptive batch cutover — does it reduce throughput alot? because we still need to keep cost reasonable.
[02:35] Julia: it can reduce throughput by up to 6% in worst-case synthetic mixes, but in your observed distribution where 70% are short queries it's actually net positive because it avoids microburst retries and reflows. so cost per effective token improves.
[02:53] Priya: our concern is also tails during peak traffic, we have these sudden surges from batch jobs that glue a bunch of long queries together. how does the kernel choose under load? any fallback?
[03:06] Leo: this is where fallback routing and model-variant hedging comes in — if the runtime detects slab-saturation for the preferred kernel it can route to a cheaper-but-predictable variant or spin up a dedicated lane. we showed a policy sample in the drive.
[03:22] Daniel: When you say cheaper variant are you talking about a quantized variant or a smaller model? how does latency compare?
[03:29] Julia: primarily a quantized variant; latency is slightly higher on median but the tail is tighter, which is desirable for TTFT-sensitive UIs. smaller model option is last-resort for severe saturation.
[03:38] [03:38] Samir: quick interjection — one ask from legal was about determinism for audit logs when we switch variants. we need to keep traceability in the logs.
[03:48] Mike: yes we need a clear signal in the trace so our incident ops can correlate spikes with routing decisions.
[03:55] Julia: trace id tagging is included — model_variant and kernel_id are emitted with each request, plus a routing_reason field. we'll include sample log lines in the SOC2 snippet.
[04:07] [04:07] Priya: awesome. can we talk about the test plan? last week the test didn't replicate the 99th because our traffic sample was different.
[04:18] Julia: planned matrix — we do three replays: 1) production-sampled replay (your anonymized sample), 2) synthetic microburst overlay where we inject 300 concurrent short sessions, 3) edge-case long-tail with mixed-seqlen spikes. for each we capture median, p95, p99 TTFT, handshake counts, and kv-eviction events.
[04:40] Daniel: capture format? CSV OK? we want to correlate with our APM traces.
[04:45] Julia: CSV plus JSON trace payloads with the model_variant/kernel_id tags. i'll make sure the schema matches your APM.
[04:53] [04:53] Speaker 2 (Samir): timeline wise?
[04:55] Julia: run the three tests by Monday (2026-07-06), share results and a short triage doc. if p99 still bad we'll attempt a small runtime change — kernel_sample_v3b — which soft pins short sessions to the early-return path under 90th traffic load.
[05:12] Mike: okay that timeline works. one more question — did you experiment with prefix/KV caching across requests? we have lots of short followups that could benefit.
[05:21] Julia: yes we enabled prefix caching in the harness, it helps median but doesn't fully solve the microburst handshake problem because the eviction boundaries are per-GPU and depend on live concurrency. caching plus smoothing helps though; we'll include both series in the results.
[05:35] Priya: any security or PII concerns with the traffic sample? we'll scrub user ids but keep timings intact.
[05:42] Samir: that's fine — we only need timing and sequence-length distribution and token counts, no PII. we'll sign the NDA addendum if needed.
[05:50] [06:00] Julia: small live demo — replayed a short snippet from your sample. (audio: keyboard noise) notice at 00:18 the KV eviction triggers and causes a 33ms spike. here with kernel_sample_v3 that disappears — median stays roughly the same but the 99th drops about 110ms in this view.
[06:18] Daniel: hmm that looks promising. is kernel_sample_v3 heavy on GPU memory? because our dedicated footprint is tight.
[06:25] Julia: marginally — we had to keep a slightly larger prefetch window for the early-return path, about +2% VRAM on the same model. not dramatic but something to note.
[06:36] Mike: can you quantify cost impact if we enable early-return for 70% of requests?
[06:42] Leo: rough ballpark we simulated — cost per 1M tokens goes down 4-7% because fewer retries and less microburst throttling, but operational costs might tick depending on capacity headroom. we'll put numbers in the benchmark sheet.
[06:56] [07:00] Priya: another angle — heatmap of sequence lengths you asked for, we'll upload by Sunday. it's mostly sub-64 but there's a fat tail of long analytics queries once a day.
[07:12] Samir: perfect, that distribution is exactly what drives our policy decisions.
[07:17] Julia: one more nuance — streaming handshake: if a request starts as short then gets extended (user continues typing), the runtime may need to convert the early-return path into full-attention midstream which is expensive. kernel_sample_v3 has a midstream-upgrade guard that tries to amortize the conversion. it's not perfect but reduces conversion spikes.
[07:40] Alicia: for product roadmapping, we want to know how often conversions happen. can you log conversion counts per session?
[07:47] Julia: yes, conversion_count per session will be emitted.
[07:50] [08:05] Daniel: any known regressions with longer prompts? we can't accept hallucination degradation.
[08:11] Julia: no model changes — just runtime routing. quality should be invariant. but we'll run a prompt-regression eval against your golden set as a safety net.
[08:21] Mike: good. how about the fallback routing mechanics — if we route to quantized variant and a customer complains about quality, is there an auto-fallback?
[08:31] Leo: policy supports immediate fallback to full-precision on error or if confidence drops below threshold. also, request-level tags let you replicate the problematic request in a safe env.
[08:42] [08:42] Priya: can that policy be per-tenant? we need different tolerance for our fraud detection and for customer support chat.
[08:50] Julia: yes per-tenant policies are supported; we'll provide a sample YAML.
[08:55] Samir: quick pause — legal and procurement asked about SLA implications if we trigger hedging frequently. it might need a dedicated SLO.
[09:05] Mike: right we need to know if hedging could affect our billing predictability.
[09:10] Samir: we'll model that in the cost sheet. Leo will draft a routing policy that includes expected cost delta and a soft-override switch.
[09:20] [09:20] Julia: returning to tests — i also want to run a microburst test where we add 40ms synthetic network jitter to simulate your remote office; sometimes the tail is network, not runtime.
[09:29] Priya: yes please, our EU office has different perf.
[09:34] Daniel: should we also test session affinity? i think some of the spikes were because sessions bounced across GPUs.
[09:42] Julia: session affinity reduces KV eviction rates; we'll enable affinity for one test run. CPU cost is negligible, and it helps tail.
[09:51] [10:05] Mike: can you show where we annotate logs so our oncall can filter?
[10:08] Julia: sure — sample log: {timestamp, request_id, model_variant: q8, kernel_id: k_samp_v3, routing_reason: hedged_capacity, conversion_count: 1, kv_evictions: 0} — we'll deliver a log-to-APM mapping.
[10:21] [10:21] Alicia: just to be clear on accept criteria for this stage: we need median TTFT under 120ms, p95 under 300ms, p99 under 600ms for our primary user flows.
[10:33] Samir: noted — we'll aim for that with the test matrix. if we can't hit p99 target we'll propose either dedicated lanes or a pricing tier for strict TTFT.
[10:45] Priya: what's the expected turnaround if p99 fails? we can't pause production.
[10:49] Samir: immediate mitigations: enable affinity, enable conservative batching, route some percent to quantized variant. longer term: Dedicated lane commit or capacity bump.
[10:59] [11:05] Julia: small risk note — the midstream-upgrade guard is heuristic; in an extreme corner case you could see duplicate tokens if the conversion isn't timed correctly. we've validated on harness but want to watch for it.
[11:17] Daniel: if that happens we need request-level replay to reproduce.
[11:21] Julia: yes — request replay + model variant tag will let us recreate it.
[11:25] [11:35] Samir: let's capture all of this in the shared doc. immediate deliverables: Julia runs the three-test matrix and uploads CSVs; Samir sends SOC2 excerpt and sample log lines; Mike uploads anonymized seqlen histograms; Leo drafts routing policy and cost delta.
[11:50] Mike: sounds good. follow-up meeting?
[11:53] Samir: propose Thursday 2026-07-09 same time for results review, unless the data requires an earlier triage.
[11:59] Priya: that's fine. thanks everyone.
[12:03] Julia: thanks, we'll update the drive and ping in the thread.
[12:07] Samir: thanks all, bye.
